nameStory: The Spotted Towhee gets its name from the distinctive white spots scattered across its black wings and back, which help distinguish it from its close relative, the Eastern Towhee. The name 'towhee' itself comes from the bird's call, which sounds like 'tow-HEE!' Both parts of this bird's name are wonderfully descriptive of what you'll see and hear.
description: The Spotted Towhee is a large, robin-sized sparrow with striking black, white, and rusty coloring. Males have a jet-black head and back decorated with white spots, bright rufous (reddish-brown) sides, and a white belly. Females show the same pattern but with chocolate brown replacing the male's black areas. These chunky birds are about 8-9 inches long with a long tail and thick, seed-cracking bill.

idTips.label: White wing spots
idTips.description: Look for distinctive white spots scattered across the dark wings and back, visible both when perched and in flight - these spots are the key field mark that separates this species from the Eastern Towhee

idTips.label: Rusty sides
idTips.description: Bright cinnamon-orange or rust-colored flanks contrast sharply with the white belly, creating a striking three-toned appearance

idTips.label: Red eyes
idTips.description: Adults have bright red or orange-red eyes that stand out against their dark head - young birds may have brownish eyes

idTips.label: Ground scratching behavior
idTips.description: Watch for their distinctive double-scratch feeding method - they hop forward, then quickly scratch backward with both feet, making a rustling sound in dry leaves

idTips.label: Harsh call
idTips.description: Listen for a sharp 'tow-HEE!' call that may sound harsher and more varied than the Eastern Towhee's cleaner notes

habitat: Spotted Towhees prefer dense shrublands, brushy areas, and forest edges with thick understory vegetation. In New England, look for them in areas with berry-producing shrubs, overgrown fields reverting to forest, and woodland borders. They need dense cover near the ground for nesting and foraging.

seasonality.spring: Listen for their territorial calls and songs as males establish breeding territories. This is when you're most likely to spot one of these rare visitors perched conspicuously while singing.
seasonality.summer: Adults may be seen with fledgling young, still showing their distinctive foraging behavior in dense brush. Look for family groups scratching through leaf litter together.
seasonality.fall: Migration period when Spotted Towhees are most likely to appear in New England as vagrants from western populations. Watch for them at bird feeders and in berry-rich areas.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in New England during winter, but any sightings would likely be at feeders or in dense, sheltered shrublands with available food sources.

funFact: Until 1995, the Spotted Towhee and Eastern Towhee were considered the same species called the Rufous-sided Towhee, but scientists discovered they were different enough to split them into two separate species - so if you spot one in New England, you're seeing a bird that didn't officially 'exist' until the mid-1990s!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the much more common Eastern Towhee, but the Spotted Towhee's white wing and back spots are the dead giveaway - Eastern Towhees are solid black (males) or brown (females) on top with no spots. Memory trick: 'Spotted' is right in the name, and if you see the spots, you've found the rarity!
contextualKnowledge: Spotted Towhees are primarily western North American birds, making any New England sighting quite special and noteworthy. They were once called 'Oregon Towhees' in some regions. The recent taxonomic split from Eastern Towhees means older field guides may not show them as separate species.
compareHints: Spotted Towhees differ from their close relative the Eastern Towhee primarily by those diagnostic white spots on wings and back - Eastern Towhees lack these spots entirely. Both species share the same basic color pattern of dark upperparts, rusty sides, and white belly, but only the Spotted Towhee looks 'polka-dotted' from above. The Green-tailed Towhee, another genus member, is much grayer overall with a distinctive rusty cap.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eastern Towhees are the only Pipilo towhee species in New England - their closest relatives are the Spotted Towhee of the west (which has white spots on the back instead of solid coloring) and the Green-tailed Towhee (which is greenish with a rusty cap).
Unlike its cousin the Eastern Towhee which is boldly patterned in black, white, and rufous with no green coloring, the Green-tailed Towhee is much smaller and more subtly colored overall.
